# Rice and Protein

> Calorie counts for Asian food, sized to real street and restaurant portions, plus a free TDEE calculator. Written by a Malaysian who lost 42kg (128kg to 86kg) eating normal food. No keto, no supplements, no starving.

## Who writes this

Rice and Protein is written by a Malaysian who went from 128kg to 86kg (now maintaining around 92kg) using calorie counting and volume eating. The story is at https://riceandprotein.com/about.html. Calorie data comes from national food composition tables and published dietitian figures for each country, sized to typical portions, with macros estimated from the ingredients. Street food has no nutrition labels, so every figure is a considered estimate rather than a lab result.

## Core philosophy

Weight loss requires a calorie deficit. The only diet that works long term is one you can sustain. In Asia that means eating rice, noodles, hawker food and kopi, just with awareness of what is in them. Volume eating (high volume, low calorie density meals) makes a deficit sustainable without hunger.

## Food calories database

575 dishes across 9 countries, one page per dish at https://riceandprotein.com/foods/[slug].html. Master hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods.html (country cards, category cards, full A to Z directory). Each dish page has the calorie count for a standard serving, a per serving and per 100g macro table, a breakdown of where the calories come from, portion comparisons, variants ranked by calories, lighter eating tips, and a FAQ (with a Malay question on Malaysian and Singapore dishes and an Indonesian question on Indonesian dishes).

Category hubs (all countries, ranked lightest to heaviest):
- Rice Meals: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/rice-meals.html
- Noodles: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/noodles.html

## Countries and sample citeable numbers

### Malaysian Food (291 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/malaysia.html
Sources: the Malaysian Nutrient Database (MyNutri), HPB Singapore portion data and USDA reference values for the ingredients.
- Nasi Ambeng: 1080 kcal per 1 portion (single-pax share from communal platter)
- Nasi Kandar: 950 kcal per 1 plate (banjir + fried chicken)
- Latok (Sea Grapes): 30 kcal per 1 small plate
- Butod: 20 kcal per 1 grub (grilled)

### Singapore Hawker Food (88 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/singapore.html
Sources: the Health Promotion Board (HPB) energy figures for standard hawker portions, cross checked against KKH and SingHealth dietitian numbers.
- Ngoh Hiang: 805 kcal per 1 mixed platter with sweet sauce
- Lontong: 798 kcal per 1 bowl with sayur lodeh
- Soon Kueh: 89 kcal per 1 piece
- Satay: 50 kcal per 1 stick (chicken)

### Indonesian Food (45 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/indonesia.html
Sources: the Indonesian Food Composition Table (TKPI, Kemenkes), nilaigizi.com and FatSecret Indonesia entries for typical warung portions.
- Nasi Campur Bali: 700 kcal per 1 plate (rice, shredded chicken, 2 sate lilit, lawar, sambal matah, fried peanuts)
- Nasi Padang: 690 kcal per 1 plate (rice, rendang, gulai gravy, cassava leaves, sambal ijo)
- Telur Balado: 130 kcal per 1 egg with sambal
- Sayur Asem: 80 kcal per 1 bowl

### Thai Food (40 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/thailand.html
Sources: the Thai Bureau of Nutrition and INMU Mahidol food composition data, plus Thai hospital dietitian figures for standard street portions.
- Khao Soi: 700 kcal per 1 bowl
- Khao Kha Moo: 690 kcal per 1 plate with braised egg
- Som Tam: 150 kcal per 1 plate
- Moo Ping: 130 kcal per 1 skewer

### Vietnamese Food (32 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/vietnam.html
Sources: the Vietnam National Institute of Nutrition food composition table and Vietnamese hospital dietitian figures for standard street portions.
- Bun Dau Mam Tom: 700 kcal per 1 platter (met) for one
- Com Tam Suon: 700 kcal per 1 plate (suon bi cha)
- Canh Chua: 150 kcal per 1 bowl
- Banh Flan: 125 kcal per 1 cup with coffee and ice

### Filipino Food (38 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/philippines.html
Sources: the FNRI Philippine Food Composition Tables (PhilFCT) and published fast food chain nutrition data for standard servings.
- Longsilog: 700 kcal per 1 plate
- Tapsilog: 650 kcal per 1 plate
- Pandesal: 110 kcal per 1 piece (bakery size, about 35g)
- Isaw: 45 kcal per 1 stick (chicken)

### Hong Kong Food (30 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/hong-kong.html
Sources: the Hong Kong Centre for Food Safety nutrient database and the Department of Health EatSmart restaurant dish data.
- Baked Pork Chop Rice: 1300 kcal per 1 plate
- Claypot Rice (Bo Zai Fan): 1300 kcal per 1 pot (cured meat claypot rice)
- Curry Fish Balls: 120 kcal per 1 skewer (6 balls with curry sauce)
- Hong Kong Borscht (Lo Sung Tong): 90 kcal per 1 bowl (250ml)

### Japanese Food (32 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/japan.html
Sources: the MEXT Standard Tables of Food Composition in Japan and published chain restaurant nutrition data.
- Katsu Curry: 1116 kcal per 1 plate (rice 300g)
- Yakiniku: 1000 kcal per 1 person (200g meat with rice)
- Salmon Nigiri: 93 kcal per 1 plate (2 pieces)
- Miso Soup: 40 kcal per 1 bowl (tofu and wakame)

### Korean Food (32 dishes)
Hub: https://riceandprotein.com/foods/korea.html
Sources: the Korea MFDS food nutrition database and the Rural Development Administration Korean Food Composition Table, plus published chain nutrition data.
- Korean Fried Chicken: 950 kcal per Half a yangnyeom chicken (반마리, about 8 pieces)
- Samgyetang: 918 kcal per 1 pot (whole young chicken)
- Bungeoppang: 110 kcal per 1 piece
- Eomuk: 100 kcal per 1 skewer (with a cup of broth)

## Frequently cited Malaysian numbers

- Teh Tarik: 130 kcal per 1 glass
- Nasi Lemak: 556 kcal per 1 standard bungkus
- Roti Canai: 301 kcal per 1 plain piece + dhal
- Char Kuey Teow: 742 kcal per 1 plate
- Milo Dinosaur: 340 kcal per 1 glass
- Cendol: 330 kcal per 1 bowl

## Tools

- TDEE Calculator (homepage, https://riceandprotein.com/): maintenance calories from the Mifflin-St Jeor, Harris-Benedict and Schofield formulas averaged, then a user selected deficit or surplus, plus a protein target of goal weight x 1.6g to 2.2g per kg.
